title: FinTech, Lesson 2: CAC, LTV and payback - is each customer profitable or not
subtitle: How to compute the cost of acquiring a customer, the value they bring, and why the LTV/CAC ratio says less than the payback period
whyItMatters: A product can grow very fast and still go bankrupt, if every new customer takes out more money than they bring in. This is the calculation that decides which of the two happens, and it is the first one an investor asks about when reviewing a funding round.
openingQuestion: A company spends 5bn on marketing in the quarter and adds 25,000 customers, of whom 5,000 arrived organically without any advertising. What is CAC?
openingOptions: Cannot be computed without knowing how many of them are still active after three months
explanation: CAC is divided only by the customers that spending actually brought in: 5bn / 20,000 = VND 250,000. Dividing by all 25,000 gives VND 200,000 and makes CAC look better than it is, because those 5,000 arrived without costing a thing - they are not the product of that spend. This is the most common way growth metrics get dressed up, and it is the first place an experienced investor will push back. The rule: the numerator contains only spending genuinely aimed at attracting new customers, and the denominator only the customers those costs produced.

realWorldExample.description: Many apps spent VND 300,000-800,000 to acquire a first-time borrower, while the first loan was only VND 2-3m and the interest earned in that cycle came to less than VND 200,000. The model only broke even if the borrower came back a second and a third time - so the whole problem shifted from 'win the customer' to 'keep the customer', and the companies that did not work that out in time shut down.

quiz.question: Which customers belong in the denominator of CAC?
options: Every customer who is active as at the end of the reporting period
Every new customer registered during the reporting period
Only the new customers who came from the acquisition spending
New customers who have completed at least one fee-generating transaction
quiz.explanation: Folding organic arrivals into the denominator pushes CAC artificially low. Someone who arrived at no cost is not a result of that spend, so including them credits the marketing budget with customers it never bought. Counting all active customers at period end mixes in everyone acquired in earlier periods, and requiring a first paid transaction measures activation rather than acquisition - a useful metric, but a different one.

quiz.question: What is LTV computed from?
options: Average transaction value times transactions per month
Average revenue per customer times the months they stay
The total amount the customer has topped up
Gross profit per customer, not revenue
quiz.explanation: Using revenue instead of gross profit inflates LTV by exactly the cost to serve - and in fintech, transaction processing costs and risk costs are far from trivial. Total top-ups measure money passing through rather than money earned. The revenue-times-months version is the most tempting error because it is nearly right: it has the correct shape and the wrong first term.

quiz.question: Why does the payback period matter more than the LTV/CAC ratio?
options: Because LTV is spread over years, while the cash has to go out today
Because LTV/CAC is not a metric found in any accounting standard, so it cannot be trusted
Because the payback period is easier to compute and needs no historical data
Because international investors only accept metrics expressed on a monthly basis
quiz.explanation: An LTV/CAC of 3 sounds very healthy, but if it takes 30 months to recover the CAC then the company has to fund that spend out of capital for 30 months. That is how a company with a beautiful LTV/CAC ratio still runs out of money. Payback is not the easier calculation either - it needs the same cohort data - and neither metric appears in an accounting standard, so that cannot be what separates them.

quiz.question: CAC is VND 250,000 and gross profit is VND 25,000 per customer per month. How long until payback?
options: 6 months (dividing by revenue)
25 months (dividing by the wrong unit)
Not enough data to compute it
quiz.explanation: 250,000 / 25,000 = 10 months. The churn rate affects LTV, but the payback period only needs the monthly gross profit of the customers who are still there.

quiz.question: Which sign shows that growth is being bought with money rather than earned with the product?
options: Marketing spend rising more slowly than revenue
Active users growing faster than app downloads
CAC rising steadily quarter after quarter while LTV stands still
Second-month return rate higher than in the previous quarter
quiz.explanation: Escalating CAC while the value of each customer is unchanged means the easy-to-persuade customers have run out, and the company is paying progressively more for a progressively worse-fitting group. The other three all point the other way: spend growing slower than revenue, activation improving relative to downloads, and retention improving are each evidence that the product is doing the work.

practicePrompt.question: CAC is VND 900,000, each customer brings VND 60,000 of gross profit per month, and monthly churn is 4%. Which number is the most worrying?
options: Payback of 15 months, longer than what counts as healthy
LTV over CAC of 1.67, so the model is fine
Churn of 4% is a very good level for fintech
LTV of VND 1.5m shows the customers are valuable
practicePrompt.explanation: LTV = 60,000 / 4% = VND 1.5m, so LTV/CAC = 1.67 - already below the 3 usually treated as healthy. But the more worrying figure is the payback period: 900,000 / 60,000 = 15 months of cash sitting outside the company before a single customer pays for themselves. LTV is a multi-year number that assumes the customer stays long enough; payback is real cash and it determines how much extra capital the company has to raise in order to grow. As for 4% monthly churn, that means losing nearly half the customer base each year - a problem, not a strength.

keyTakeaways: CAC = acquisition spend / the customers that spend brought in. Do not fold organic arrivals into the denominator.
LTV is computed on gross profit, not revenue - otherwise the cost to serve disappears from the calculation.
The payback period says more than the LTV/CAC ratio, because it is about cash rather than about a multi-year figure.
CAC creeping up while LTV stands still is the sign that the easy customer pool has run dry.

summary.keyIdea: The payback period says more than the LTV/CAC ratio, because it is about cash
summary.formula: Payback period = CAC / gross profit per customer per month
summary.commonMistake: Computing LTV on revenue instead of gross profit, which makes the cost to serve vanish from the calculation.
summary.action: For a product you know, estimate CAC and monthly gross profit, then divide to get the number of months to payback.

application.title: Check the denominator of CAC
application.message: When you read a CAC figure, ask immediately whether the denominator includes organic arrivals. If it does, the number is lower than reality and every conclusion built on it is skewed.
application.secondary: CAC creeping up while LTV stands still is the sign that the easy customer pool has run dry.

sections.text: User growth is the easiest thing in business to buy: you just spend enough. The only question worth asking is whether each person bought returns more than was spent on them, and how long that takes.
CAC: the price of one customer

CAC covers every cost aimed at gaining new customers - advertising, promotions, referral bonuses, the growth team's salaries - divided by the customers those costs actually brought in. The easy mistake sits in the denominator: adding in the people who found you on their own makes CAC look lower than it is.
LTV: how much the customer gives back

sections.title: Customer lifetime value
sections.equation: LTV = gross profit per month × months retained

example.title: An e-wallet user
example.explanation: If CAC is 250,000 then LTV/CAC is 1.7 - below the 3 that most funds treat as the healthy threshold.

left.label: LTV/CAC = 3
left.text: Sounds healthy, but says nothing about when the money comes back. Three years or three months both produce this same number.

right.label: Payback of 10 months
right.text: Says it plainly: the company has to fund each customer out of capital for 10 months before they start contributing.

sections.label: Why a fast-growing company still runs out of money
sections.text: Because CAC is spent today while LTV arrives over years. The faster the growth, the wider the gap between those two cash flows - which is why the companies raising round after round are usually the ones growing fastest, not the ones that are weakest.

lines: Three numbers have to be read together: CAC, gross profit per customer, and months to payback.
If you only get to ask one question about a fintech product, ask the third one.
